label: Red Grapes
desc: Cabernet to Nebbiolo — know your reds

beginner.q: Which grape forms the backbone of Bordeaux red blends?
beginner.fact: Cab Sauv dominates the left-bank Médoc — Pauillac, Saint-Estèphe and Margaux.

beginner.q: Chianti is made primarily from which grape?
beginner.fact: Sangiovese is the soul of Tuscany — it means "blood of Jupiter".

beginner.q: Pinot Noir is the signature grape of which French region?
beginner.fact: Burgundy's Côte de Nuits is arguably the world's greatest Pinot Noir terroir.

beginner.q: Malbec is most celebrated in which country?
beginner.fact: Mendoza's high altitude and sunshine transformed Malbec into an international star.

beginner.q: Which grape makes Barolo — "the King of Italian wines"?
beginner.fact: Nebbiolo is described as smelling of tar and roses, and can age for 30+ years.

beginner.q: Rioja reds are primarily made from which grape?
beginner.fact: Tempranillo is Spain's most planted red grape and means "little early one".

beginner.q: Which Australian region is most famous for old-vine Shiraz?
beginner.fact: Barossa has vines over 150 years old — producing some of the world's most concentrated Shiraz.

beginner.q: Beaujolais Nouveau is made from which grape?
beginner.fact: Gamay is the only grape allowed in Beaujolais — vinified by carbonic maceration for fresh, fruity wines.

intermediate.q: Amarone della Valpolicella is made from dried grapes — its primary variety is?
intermediate.fact: Corvina grapes are dried for months on bamboo racks in a process called "appassimento".

intermediate.q: Which single grape produces Hermitage and Crozes-Hermitage in the Northern Rhône?
intermediate.fact: The Northern Rhône is exclusively Syrah territory — no blending permitted.

intermediate.q: Primitivo in Italy is genetically identical to which American variety?
intermediate.fact: DNA testing confirmed Primitivo = Zinfandel in the 1990s. Both trace back to a Croatian grape.

intermediate.q: Which grape is considered Portugal's finest red, used in Port and dry wines?
intermediate.fact: Touriga Nacional is prized for its intense floral aromas and deep colour.

intermediate.q: Tannat is the signature grape of which South American country?
intermediate.fact: Uruguay made Tannat its national grape — it thrives in the Atlantic-influenced climate.

intermediate.q: Châteauneuf-du-Pape blends up to 18 varieties — which typically dominates?
intermediate.fact: Grenache often makes up 60–80% of a CdP blend, giving warmth and red fruit character.

intermediate.q: Blaufränkisch is Austria's finest red. What is it called in Germany?
intermediate.fact: Blaufränkisch/Lemberger is spicy, structured and capable of great ageing in Burgenland.

intermediate.q: Pinotage is a unique grape created in which country?
intermediate.fact: Pinotage is a South African cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsaut, created at Stellenbosch University in 1925.

expert.q: Aglianico del Vulture DOCG comes from which Italian region?
expert.fact: The volcanic Mount Vulture soils of Basilicata give Aglianico extraordinary mineral depth.

expert.q: Pomerol and Saint-Émilion on Bordeaux's right bank are dominated by:
expert.fact: Pétrus — the world's most expensive wine by the bottle — is almost 100% Merlot.

expert.q: Xinomavro is a structured red grape indigenous to which country?
expert.fact: "Xinomavro" means "acid black" in Greek — it's the Nebbiolo of the Eastern Mediterranean.

expert.q: Sagrantino DOCG, with wine's highest tannin levels, is grown near:
expert.fact: Sagrantino di Montefalco is one of Italy's most powerful and age-worthy wines.

expert.q: Which grape makes the famed single-varietal wines of Priorat, Spain?
expert.fact: Old-vine Garnacha on Priorat's black slate "llicorella" produces extreme concentration.

expert.q: Nerello Mascalese grown on Etna's volcanic slopes is often compared to which Burgundy grape?
expert.fact: Etna Rosso from Nerello Mascalese shares Pinot Noir's translucency, earthiness and perfume.

beginner.q: White Burgundy (Chablis, Meursault, Puligny) is made from which grape?
beginner.fact: All white Burgundy is 100% Chardonnay — one grape, infinite expressions.

beginner.q: Marlborough, New Zealand made which grape internationally famous?
beginner.fact: Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc changed the world's palate in the 1980s with its vivid tropical character.

beginner.q: Prosecco is made from which grape variety?
beginner.fact: Glera (formerly called Prosecco) must make up at least 85% of any Prosecco DOC wine.

beginner.q: Albariño is the aromatic white grape of which Spanish region?
beginner.fact: Rías Baixas in rainy Galicia produces the most vivid and food-friendly Albariño.

beginner.q: Champagne's "Blanc de Blancs" is made exclusively from which grape?
beginner.fact: Blanc de Blancs ("white from whites") — lighter, more delicate and longer-lived than non-vintage Champagne.

beginner.q: German Riesling can range in style from:
beginner.fact: Germany's Prädikat system (Kabinett through Trockenbeerenauslese) covers dry to intensely sweet.

beginner.q: Which grape is used to make Soave DOC from Veneto, Italy?
beginner.fact: Garganega is the backbone of Soave — delicate, almondy and food-friendly.

beginner.q: Grüner Veltliner is the flagship white grape of which country?
beginner.fact: Austria's most planted grape — known for its signature white pepper note and crisp minerality.

intermediate.q: Viognier is the sole grape of which Northern Rhône appellation?
intermediate.fact: Condrieu produces the world's most exotic and heady aromatic whites — 100% Viognier.

intermediate.q: Which white grape is the primary variety in Sauternes?
intermediate.fact: Sauternes is a blend — Sémillon dominates (affected by noble rot), with Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle.

intermediate.q: Furmint is the grape at the heart of which legendary sweet wine?
intermediate.fact: Hungarian Tokaji has been made since the 17th century — praised by Napoleon and the Tsar.

intermediate.q: Palomino is the grape used to make which classic fortified wine?
intermediate.fact: Palomino Fino makes up 95%+ of the base wine for Fino and Manzanilla Sherry.

intermediate.q: Which Burgundy white appellation is known for steely, mineral, unoaked style?
intermediate.fact: Chablis sits north of the rest of Burgundy — Kimmeridgian limestone gives it unparalleled minerality.

intermediate.q: Torrontés — Argentina's aromatic white — is most expressive from which province?
intermediate.fact: Salta's extreme altitude (up to 3,000m) produces the most floral, vibrant Torrontés.

intermediate.q: Muscadet is made from which grape variety?
intermediate.fact: Melon de Bourgogne — crisp, light and perfect with oysters and seafood from the Atlantic coast.

intermediate.q: "Sur lie" ageing means the wine is aged on:
intermediate.fact: Sur lie ageing adds creaminess, complexity and autolytic (bread-dough) character to white wines.

expert.q: Rkatsiteli — one of the world's oldest cultivated vines — is from which country?
expert.fact: Georgia's 8,000-year winemaking history centres on Rkatsiteli and amber-style qvevri wines.

expert.q: In Alsace, what is an "Edelzwicker"?
opts: A blend of noble Alsatian grapes
expert.fact: Edelzwicker ("noble blend") can combine Riesling, Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer and others.

expert.q: Airén covers vast plains of La Mancha. Why is it significant?
opts: It may be the world's most planted white grape by area
It is used to make Cava
It is the base for Sherry
expert.fact: Airén's prolific yields over La Mancha's arid plains made it the most planted white grape globally for decades.

expert.q: Vernaccia di San Gimignano holds which historic Italian wine distinction?
expert.fact: Vernaccia di San Gimignano was Italy's very first DOC, awarded in 1966.

expert.q: Gewürztraminer at its most expressive typically shows which aromatic profile?
opts: Lychee, rose petal, ginger and spice
expert.fact: Gewürztraminer's hallmarks are intense lychee, Turkish delight and exotic spice aromas — often off-dry.

expert.q: Which Galician white appellation — not Rías Baixas — is known for fragrant, mineral whites from the Ribeiro valley?
expert.fact: Ribeiro is Galicia's oldest appellation — its Treixadura-dominant blends are floral, fresh and underrated.

label: Rosé
desc: Provence pink to Tavel: how rosé is made

beginner.q: How do most rosé wines get their pink colour?
opts: Brief contact between the juice and red grape skins
Mixing red and white wine in the bottle
beginner.fact: The skins sit with the juice for a few hours to a couple of days, then come out: the longer they stay, the deeper the pink.

beginner.q: Which French region is most famous for pale, dry rosé?
beginner.fact: Rosé makes up the vast majority of everything Provence produces.

beginner.q: What colour are the grapes used for most rosé?
beginner.fact: The juice of nearly all red grapes is clear. The colour is in the skins.

beginner.q: Most rosé is best enjoyed…
opts: Young and fresh, within a year or two
After ten years in the cellar
beginner.fact: Rosé is made to be drunk while its fruit is fresh.

beginner.q: What is "saignée" in rosé making?
opts: Bleeding off pink juice early from a red wine tank
Blending finished red and white wine
beginner.fact: Saignée means "bleeding": it gives a deeper pink rosé and concentrates the red wine left behind.

beginner.q: Which grape is the backbone of many Provence rosés?
beginner.fact: Grenache, often with Cinsault and Syrah, gives Provence rosé its red-berry fruit.

beginner.q: What serving temperature suits a dry rosé?
beginner.fact: Serve it chilled like a white wine to keep it crisp and refreshing.

beginner.q: In Spain, rosé is called…
beginner.fact: Rosado from Navarra and Rioja is often deeper in colour than Provence rosé. In Italy it's rosato.

intermediate.q: Tavel, a French appellation that makes only rosé, is in…
intermediate.fact: Tavel is a deeper, fuller rosé that can stand up to food like a light red.

intermediate.q: Does a paler rosé mean it's drier?
opts: No: colour comes from skin contact, not sweetness
intermediate.fact: Sweetness depends on how much sugar is left after fermentation, not on the colour.

intermediate.q: How is most rosé Champagne made?
opts: By blending a little red wine into the white base wine
By adding grape skins to each bottle
By ageing in red wine barrels
intermediate.fact: Champagne is one of the few places in Europe allowed to make rosé by blending red and white.

intermediate.q: Californian "White Zinfandel" is typically…
opts: Pale pink and off-dry to sweet
intermediate.fact: White Zinfandel became hugely popular in the 1980s and introduced many people to wine.

intermediate.q: Chiaretto, a pale Italian rosé, comes from around…
intermediate.fact: Chiaretto di Bardolino is made near Lake Garda from the same grapes as Valpolicella.

intermediate.q: Why do many rosés come in clear glass bottles?
intermediate.fact: Clear glass shows the colour but lets light in, so keep rosé out of the sun.

intermediate.q: Rosé d'Anjou from the Loire is usually…
intermediate.fact: For a dry Loire rosé, look for Rosé de Loire on the label instead.

intermediate.q: Which food is a classic match for dry Provence rosé?
intermediate.fact: Its freshness and light body suit Mediterranean dishes.

expert.q: Bandol rosé is built mainly on which grape?
expert.fact: Mourvèdre gives Bandol rosé more structure than most, so it can age a few years.

expert.q: "Vin gris" is…
opts: A very pale rosé from red grapes pressed straight away
A red wine aged in clay
expert.fact: The juice barely touches the skins, so the wine is only faintly pink.

expert.q: Navarra built its reputation on rosado made from…
expert.fact: Navarra's Garnacha rosados are fruity and deeper in colour than Provence's.

expert.q: How does direct-press rosé differ from saignée rosé?
opts: Rosé is the main aim, with skin contact only during pressing
expert.fact: Direct-press rosés tend to be the palest and most delicate.

expert.q: Which Portuguese rosé was a worldwide hit from the 1950s?
expert.fact: Mateus, in its flask-shaped bottle, was one of the world's best-selling wines.

expert.q: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a deep rosé made from…
expert.fact: Cerasuolo means cherry-red, a nod to its colour.

label: Sparkling
desc: Champagne, Prosecco, Cava: where the bubbles come from

beginner.q: Where must Champagne come from?
beginner.fact: Only sparkling wine from the Champagne region may be called Champagne.

beginner.q: Prosecco comes from which country?
beginner.fact: Prosecco is made in north-east Italy, mainly from the Glera grape.

beginner.q: Cava is a sparkling wine from…
beginner.fact: Most Cava comes from Penedès in Catalonia.

beginner.q: What does "Brut" on a sparkling wine label tell you?
beginner.fact: Brut is dry. Extra Brut and Brut Nature are drier still; Demi-Sec is sweet.

beginner.q: Where do the bubbles in Champagne come from?
opts: A second fermentation in the bottle
beginner.fact: Yeast and a little sugar are added to still wine, which ferments again in the sealed bottle and traps the gas.

beginner.q: Which grapes are the main three in Champagne?
beginner.fact: Meunier is also called Pinot Meunier.

beginner.q: How is Prosecco usually made sparkling?
opts: A second fermentation in a large pressurised tank
A second fermentation in each bottle
beginner.fact: The tank method keeps Prosecco's fresh, fruity aromas.

beginner.q: "Blanc de Blancs" means the wine is made from…
opts: A blend of red and white wine
beginner.fact: In Champagne, Blanc de Blancs is usually 100% Chardonnay.

intermediate.q: "Blanc de Noirs" is a white sparkling wine made from…
intermediate.fact: The grapes are pressed gently so the skins don't colour the juice.

intermediate.q: Non-vintage Champagne must spend at least how long in the cellar before release?
intermediate.fact: At least 12 of those months are on its lees. Vintage Champagne needs 3 years.

intermediate.q: Toasty, brioche-like aromas in Champagne come from…
opts: Time ageing on dead yeast cells (lees)
intermediate.fact: The breakdown of yeast cells is called autolysis.

intermediate.q: What is a Crémant?
opts: French sparkling wine made the Champagne way, outside Champagne
intermediate.fact: Look for Crémant de Loire, d'Alsace or de Bourgogne: often great value.

intermediate.q: "Demi-Sec" sparkling wine is…
intermediate.fact: Demi-Sec is a good match for desserts that would make a Brut taste sour.

intermediate.q: Riddling (remuage) is done to…
opts: Move the dead yeast into the neck of the bottle
intermediate.fact: The neck is then frozen and the yeast plug is popped out, which is called disgorgement.

intermediate.q: Moscato d'Asti is…
opts: Lightly sparkling, sweet and low in alcohol
intermediate.fact: It's often only around 5% alcohol.

intermediate.q: English sparkling wine does well on…
opts: Chalky soils in the south, like Champagne's
intermediate.fact: Sussex, Kent and Hampshire share chalk with Champagne.

expert.q: In sparkling wine, "dosage" is…
opts: The sugar solution added after disgorging
expert.fact: Dosage sets the final sweetness, from Brut Nature to Doux.

expert.q: The pressure inside a bottle of Champagne is roughly…
expert.fact: That's why the cork is held down with a wire cage.

expert.q: Franciacorta is Italy's traditional-method sparkling wine from…
expert.fact: Like Champagne, it's made with a second fermentation in the bottle.

expert.q: Pét-Nat (pétillant naturel) is made by…
opts: Bottling the wine before its first fermentation has finished
expert.fact: It's the oldest way of making sparkling wine, and often a little cloudy.

expert.q: A "prestige cuvée" is…
opts: A house's top wine, such as Dom Pérignon or Cristal
expert.fact: Prestige cuvées come from the best vineyards and age for years before release.

expert.q: Which is the top village classification in Champagne?
expert.fact: Seventeen villages hold Grand Cru status. Cru Bourgeois is a Bordeaux term.

label: Orange Wine
desc: White grapes made like a red: skin contact explained

beginner.q: Orange wine is made from…
opts: White grapes left on their skins
A blend of red and white wine
beginner.fact: Skin contact gives the wine its colour, texture and grip.

beginner.q: Where does orange wine's colour come from?
beginner.fact: The longer the skins stay in, the deeper the amber.

beginner.q: Orange wine often has something white wines rarely have:
beginner.fact: Tannin comes from skins and seeds, which is why reds have it and most whites don't.

beginner.q: Which country has made skin-contact white wine in clay vessels for thousands of years?
beginner.fact: Georgia's clay vessels are called qvevri.

beginner.q: Another name for orange wine is…
beginner.fact: "Amber" is common in Georgia, where the style comes from.

beginner.q: How is orange wine usually best served?
opts: Cool, around 12–14°C, like a light red
beginner.fact: Too cold and the tannin feels harsh; slightly cool shows its texture.

beginner.q: Orange wine's grip makes it good with…
opts: Richly flavoured food, like spiced dishes and hard cheese
beginner.fact: Its tannin and savoury flavours stand up to bold food.

beginner.q: Is orange wine the same as rosé?
opts: No: rosé uses red grapes, orange wine uses white grapes
beginner.fact: Both involve skin contact, but with different coloured grapes.

intermediate.q: Qvevri are…
opts: Large clay vessels buried in the ground
intermediate.fact: Burying them keeps the fermenting wine at a steady, cool temperature.

intermediate.q: Which north-east Italian area near Slovenia is famous for orange wine?
intermediate.fact: Producers around Oslavia in Collio led the modern revival.

intermediate.q: Skin contact for orange wine can last…
opts: From a few days to many months
intermediate.fact: Longer contact gives more colour, tannin and savoury character.

intermediate.q: Ribolla Gialla is a grape famous for…
opts: Orange wines in Friuli and Slovenia
intermediate.fact: Its thick skins suit long skin contact.

intermediate.q: Rkatsiteli is a white grape from…
intermediate.fact: It's one of Georgia's most planted grapes, often made in qvevri.

intermediate.q: Why can orange wine taste more savoury than fruity?
opts: Skin contact and air add tea-like, nutty flavours and grip
intermediate.fact: Many describe it as tasting of dried apricot, tea and spice.

intermediate.q: Many orange wines are also made with…
opts: Minimal intervention: wild yeasts and little added sulphur
intermediate.fact: The style is closely linked with the natural wine movement.

intermediate.q: Orange wine's colour ranges from…
intermediate.fact: Colour depends on the grape and how long the skins stay in.

expert.q: Josko Gravner is known for…
opts: Reviving orange wine made in qvevri in Friuli
expert.fact: He began fermenting in Georgian qvevri in the early 2000s.

expert.q: Why does skin contact add tannin?
opts: Tannins in the skins and seeds dissolve into the fermenting wine
Tannin powder is required by law
expert.fact: It's the same process that gives red wine its tannin.

expert.q: Georgian qvevri winemaking was added to UNESCO's heritage list in…
expert.fact: It's on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

expert.q: Which Slovenian region across the border from Collio also makes skin-contact whites?
expert.fact: Brda and Collio are really one landscape divided by a border.

expert.q: Pinot Grigio left on its skins gives a copper-coloured wine called…
expert.fact: Ramato means "auburn" or copper in Italian.

expert.q: In Georgia, skin-contact white wine is usually called…
expert.fact: Georgian producers prefer "amber" to "orange".

beginner.q: A fortified wine has…
beginner.fact: Fortified wines are usually 15–22% alcohol.

beginner.q: Port comes from which country?
beginner.fact: The grapes grow in the Douro Valley; the wine traditionally ages in Vila Nova de Gaia, across the river from Porto.

beginner.q: Sherry comes from around which Spanish town?
beginner.fact: "Sherry" is the English version of Jerez.

beginner.q: Sauternes is a sweet wine from…
beginner.fact: Sauternes is a small area in the south of Bordeaux.

beginner.q: Noble rot (botrytis) helps make sweet wine by…
opts: Shrivelling the grapes and concentrating their sugar
beginner.fact: It's a helpful fungus that needs misty mornings and dry afternoons.

beginner.q: Ice wine is made from grapes that…
beginner.fact: Pressing frozen grapes leaves the ice behind and squeezes out sweet, concentrated juice.

beginner.q: Is all Sherry sweet?
opts: No: Fino and Manzanilla are bone dry
beginner.fact: Dry Fino and Manzanilla are great with salty snacks like olives and almonds.

beginner.q: A classic match for Port is…
beginner.fact: Sweet and salty is one of food and wine's great partnerships.

intermediate.q: Why is spirit added to Port during fermentation?
opts: To stop fermentation and keep the grapes' natural sugar
intermediate.fact: The spirit kills the yeast before it has turned all the sugar into alcohol.

intermediate.q: Tawny Port gets its colour and nutty flavour from…
intermediate.fact: A 10- or 20-year-old tawny shows the average age of the blend.

intermediate.q: In Fino Sherry, "flor" is…
opts: A layer of yeast that protects the wine from air
intermediate.fact: Flor gives Fino its fresh, bready, salty tang.

intermediate.q: Pedro Ximénez (PX) Sherry is…
opts: Intensely sweet, made from sun-dried grapes
intermediate.fact: Try it poured over vanilla ice cream.

intermediate.q: Tokaji Aszú comes from…
intermediate.fact: Its sweetness comes from noble-rotted grapes.

intermediate.q: Madeira is famous for…
opts: Being heated as it ages, which makes it extremely long-lived
intermediate.fact: Opened bottles of Madeira keep for months.

intermediate.q: Vintage Port is…
opts: Made only in declared years and aged mostly in bottle
Any Port from a single month
intermediate.fact: It often needs decades to soften, and should be decanted off its sediment.

intermediate.q: When pairing, a dessert wine should be…
opts: At least as sweet as the dessert
intermediate.fact: A wine drier than the dessert tastes thin and sour next to it.

expert.q: The solera system is…
opts: Fractional blending of older and younger wine through tiers of barrels
expert.fact: Each bottle of Sherry contains a little of very old wine.

expert.q: Which grape makes Sauternes alongside Sauvignon Blanc?
expert.fact: Sémillon's thin skins are especially prone to noble rot.

expert.q: Late Bottled Vintage (LBV) Port spends how long in wood before bottling?
expert.fact: LBV is ready to drink sooner than Vintage Port.

expert.q: A Vin Doux Naturel such as Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is…
opts: A sweet wine fortified to stop fermentation
expert.fact: France's answer to Port's method, usually with Muscat or Grenache.

expert.q: Trockenbeerenauslese is made from…
opts: Individually picked grapes shrivelled by noble rot
expert.fact: It's among the rarest and sweetest German wines.

expert.q: Amontillado Sherry starts life as…
opts: A Fino, then ages further without flor
expert.fact: Once the flor dies, air turns the wine amber and nutty.

beginner.q: Which French region produces famous Cabernet Sauvignon-based reds?
beginner.fact: Bordeaux's left-bank Médoc (Pauillac, Margaux) is the historic home of great Cabernet.

beginner.q: True Champagne can only come from which country?
beginner.fact: The Champagne appellation is legally protected — only wines from this specific French region can use the name.

beginner.q: The Barossa Valley is a world-famous wine region in which country?
beginner.fact: Barossa in South Australia is renowned for old-vine Shiraz, some vines over 150 years old.

beginner.q: Chianti Classico is produced in which Italian region?
beginner.fact: Chianti Classico sits in the hills between Florence and Siena — the ancient heart of Chianti.

beginner.q: Rioja is a celebrated wine region in which country?
beginner.fact: Rioja's tiered Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva system is Spain's most recognised appellation.

beginner.q: Marlborough, famed for Sauvignon Blanc, is in which country?
beginner.fact: Marlborough at the top of New Zealand's South Island has perfect cool-climate conditions.

beginner.q: Napa Valley is the most prestigious wine region in which country?
beginner.fact: Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon commands prices rivalling Bordeaux — and often outscores them in blind tastings.

beginner.q: Douro Valley is Portugal's greatest wine region, famous for:
beginner.fact: The terraced schist vineyards of the Douro produce classic Port and some of Europe's finest dry reds.

intermediate.q: Which Bordeaux appellation on the "right bank" is home to Pétrus?
intermediate.fact: Pomerol's clay soils are ideal for Merlot. Pétrus, the world's most expensive wine, comes from here.

intermediate.q: Piedmont's "Langhe" hills are home to which two great DOCG wines?
intermediate.fact: The Langhe is the beating heart of Nebbiolo — Barolo (bigger) and Barbaresco (more elegant).

intermediate.q: Which German region produces the finest Rieslings on steep slate slopes?
intermediate.fact: Mosel's impossibly steep terraces face south to maximise sunshine in this cool climate.

intermediate.q: Priorat — known for powerful Garnacha — is in which Spanish region?
intermediate.fact: Priorat's unique black slate and quartz soils ("llicorella") give its wines extraordinary mineral depth.

intermediate.q: Willamette Valley in Oregon, USA is most celebrated for:
intermediate.fact: Oregon's cool, rainy Willamette Valley produces Pinot Noirs that rival Burgundy at a fraction of the price.

intermediate.q: Stellenbosch is a world-class wine region in which country?
intermediate.fact: Stellenbosch — just outside Cape Town — is home to some of Africa's finest Cabernet Sauvignon.

intermediate.q: Mendoza, at altitude in the Andes foothills, is in which country?
intermediate.fact: Mendoza produces 70% of Argentina's wine — its high altitude and sunshine are perfect for Malbec.

intermediate.q: Which region of Italy makes the sparkling Franciacorta using the traditional method?
intermediate.fact: Franciacorta DOCG near Brescia is Italy's answer to Champagne — bottle-fermented and aged on lees.

expert.q: How many Premiers Crus Classés châteaux exist in the 1855 Bordeaux Classification?
expert.fact: The original 1855 list had 4 Premiers Crus; Mouton Rothschild was promoted in 1973 — the only change in 170 years.

expert.q: Gevrey-Chambertin is a Grand Cru commune in which sub-region of Burgundy?
expert.fact: The Côte de Nuits runs from Gevrey-Chambertin to Nuits-Saint-Georges — the world's greatest Pinot Noir strip.

expert.q: Tokaj wine region historically spans Hungary and which other country?
expert.fact: A small strip of the historic Tokaj region lies in Slovakia, where Tokajský wines are still produced.

expert.q: Tokaj wine region historically spans Hungary and which other country?
expert.fact: A small strip of the historic Tokaj region lies in Slovakia, where Tokajský wines are still produced.

expert.q: The Mosel valley in Germany borders which two countries?
expert.fact: The Mosel river rises in France, passes through Luxembourg, and joins the Rhine at Koblenz in Germany.

expert.q: Vinho Verde DOC in Portugal means "green wine" — what does this actually refer to?
opts: The wine is young/fresh, not the colour
Wines from the Minho green hills only
expert.fact: "Verde" means young — Vinho Verde is meant to be drunk young and fresh. Red and white versions both exist.

expert.q: Coonawarra in South Australia is famous for its "terra rossa" soils over limestone. What does it grow best?
expert.fact: Coonawarra's red terra rossa topsoil over cool limestone produces structured, elegant Cabernet of outstanding quality.

beginner.q: What does "tannins" refer to in red wine?
opts: The drying, grippy sensation in your mouth
beginner.fact: Tannins come from grape skins, seeds, stems and oak barrels — they create structure and allow ageing.

beginner.q: When a wine is described as "dry", it means:
beginner.fact: A dry wine has had almost all its grape sugar fermented into alcohol. The opposite of sweet.

beginner.q: What does "finish" or "length" mean in wine tasting?
opts: How long flavours linger after you swallow
The colour depth of the wine
beginner.fact: A "long finish" (20+ seconds of lingering flavour) is a hallmark of great wine.

beginner.q: Why do you swirl wine in the glass?
opts: To release aromas by oxygenating the wine
beginner.fact: Swirling vaporises aromatic compounds so your nose can detect them more easily.

beginner.q: What does "terroir" mean?
opts: The complete natural environment of a vineyard
beginner.fact: Terroir (soil, climate, slope, aspect, microbiome) is what makes one plot taste different from its neighbour.

beginner.q: A wine with "high acidity" will taste:
beginner.fact: Acidity makes your mouth water — it's the backbone of fresh, food-friendly wine. Low acidity feels "flabby".

beginner.q: What is "body" in wine tasting terms?
opts: How heavy and full the wine feels in your mouth
The colour and opacity of the wine
The alcohol level on the label
beginner.fact: Body is largely determined by alcohol and extract — think of skimmed milk (light) vs double cream (full).

beginner.q: What does "oak influence" typically add to a wine?
opts: Vanilla, toast, spice and rounded texture
beginner.fact: New French oak adds vanilla and spice; American oak is more coconut and sawdust. Both soften and round wine.

intermediate.q: What is "malolactic fermentation" (MLF)?
opts: Converting tart malic acid to softer lactic acid
Fermenting in barrels instead of tanks
intermediate.fact: MLF makes wines rounder and creamier — virtually all reds and many oaked whites undergo it.

intermediate.q: What do "legs" or "tears" on a glass actually indicate?
opts: Higher alcohol or residual sugar (Marangoni effect)
The wine is ready to drink
intermediate.fact: Legs are caused by the Marangoni effect — they indicate higher alcohol or sugar, NOT quality.

intermediate.q: A wine described as "bretty" has:
opts: A barnyard, leather or Band-Aid aroma from yeast
intermediate.fact: Brettanomyces yeast creates "brett" — at low levels complex, at high levels a wine fault.

intermediate.q: What is "reduction" in wine?
opts: A sulphury or struck-match character from lack of oxygen
intermediate.fact: Reduction occurs when wine hasn't had enough oxygen — it often blows off with swirling or decanting.

intermediate.q: Why do winemakers "punch down" during red wine fermentation?
opts: To submerge the grape skin cap and extract colour and tannin
intermediate.fact: Grape skins float to form a "cap" — breaking it up maximises colour, tannin and flavour extraction.

intermediate.q: "Volatile acidity" (VA) at high levels creates which fault?
intermediate.fact: VA is mostly acetic acid — above ~1.4 g/L it becomes a detectable and unpleasant fault.

intermediate.q: What does decanting an old red wine primarily achieve?
opts: Separates sediment and allows the wine to breathe
intermediate.fact: Old wines should be gently decanted to remove sediment; young tannic reds benefit from the aeration.

intermediate.q: "Phenolic ripeness" in red wines most directly affects:
intermediate.fact: Fully phenolically ripe tannins are silky and round; underripe phenolics produce hard, astringent tannins.

expert.q: The WSET Systematic Approach to Tasting covers which main categories?
expert.fact: The WSET SAT is the global standard used from Level 2 through the Diploma and MW.

expert.q: What is the purpose of "dosage" in Champagne production?
opts: To adjust final sweetness after disgorging
To clarify the wine by riddling
expert.fact: Dosage (wine + sugar added after disgorgement) determines Brut, Extra Brut, Demi-Sec etc.

expert.q: "Whole-cluster fermentation" in Pinot Noir contributes:
opts: Spice, savouriness and structural tannin from stems
expert.fact: Stems can add a forest floor or spicy savoury complexity — used by top Burgundy producers like Rousseau.

expert.q: Which compound primarily causes the "cat's pee" aroma in Sauvignon Blanc?
expert.fact: Pyrazines create green, herbaceous, vegetal aromas — especially from cool-climate Sauvignon Blanc.

expert.q: What is "cryoextraction" used for in sweet wine production?
opts: Freezing grapes to concentrate sugars and flavours
expert.fact: Cryoextraction mimics natural freezing — water in the grape freezes first, leaving concentrated sugary juice.

expert.q: The "Brix" scale measures:
opts: Potential alcohol from sugar content in grape juice
expert.fact: Each degree Brix roughly corresponds to 0.55% potential alcohol — winemakers use it to decide harvest timing.

beginner.q: Which wine is the classic pairing with oysters?
beginner.fact: The mineral, saline acidity of Chablis mirrors the salinity of oysters — a textbook match.

beginner.q: What is the classic pairing with Sauternes?
beginner.fact: Sauternes' sweetness and acidity balance the richness of foie gras — one of food and wine's great marriages.

beginner.q: Which wine would you choose with a rich rack of lamb?
beginner.fact: The tannins and body of a full-bodied red cut through lamb fat and cleanse the palate beautifully.

beginner.q: Why does sparkling wine pair so well with fried food?
opts: The bubbles and acidity cut through oil
beginner.fact: Champagne and fish & chips is genuinely brilliant — the acidity and bubbles dissolve the grease.

beginner.q: A light, crisp Pinot Grigio pairs best with:
beginner.fact: Match wine weight to food weight — light wine, light dish. Pinot Grigio would be overwhelmed by heavy food.

beginner.q: "What grows together, goes together" suggests:
opts: Regional food and wine pairings often work best
Only French wine with French food
Coastal wines taste of the sea
beginner.fact: Italian wine with Italian food, Rioja with tapas — regional pairings are almost always a safe starting point.

beginner.q: Which wine works best with a simple green salad with vinaigrette?
beginner.fact: Match acid with acid — the wine's acidity needs to meet or exceed the vinaigrette, or it will taste flat.

beginner.q: Champagne is traditionally served as an aperitif. Why does it work so well?
opts: High acidity and bubbles stimulate appetite
High sugar gives energy before the meal
It is the most expensive option
beginner.fact: Bubbles and acidity cleanse and stimulate the palate — making Champagne a perfect appetite opener.

intermediate.q: Tannic red wines should generally be avoided with:
intermediate.fact: Tannin reacts with fish oils to create an unpleasant metallic or bitter taste on the palate.

intermediate.q: A wine with high residual sugar pairs best with:
intermediate.fact: Sweetness in wine tames the heat of chilli — an off-dry Riesling with Thai curry is a classic example.

intermediate.q: For a chocolate dessert, the wine should be:
intermediate.fact: If the wine is less sweet than the dessert, it will taste thin and acidic — always match or exceed sweetness.

intermediate.q: Umami-rich foods (mushrooms, aged cheese, truffle) tend to:
opts: Amplify tannins and acidity in wine
intermediate.fact: Umami intensifies perceived tannin and acidity — choose lower-tannin, lower-acid wines with umami-heavy dishes.

intermediate.q: Why does Sancerre pair so well with Crottin de Chavignol goat's cheese?
opts: Both from Loire Valley — share herbaceous, mineral qualities
intermediate.fact: This textbook regional pairing — the cheese and wine share the same mineral, grassy Loire terroir.

intermediate.q: The "bridge ingredient" technique means:
opts: Using a shared ingredient in the sauce to link wine and dish
Using the cooking wine as the drinking wine
Matching wine colour to sauce colour
intermediate.fact: A lemon butter sauce bridges sole to white Burgundy; a red wine reduction bridges beef to Pomerol.

intermediate.q: Rich, fatty foods (duck confit, foie gras) pair well with wines that have:
opts: High acidity to cut through the fat
High tannins to overwhelm the fat
intermediate.fact: Acidity acts as a palate cleanser — it cuts through fat and makes each bite taste fresh again.

intermediate.q: Which classic pairing breaks the "tannin + fish = metallic" rule?
opts: Fatty tuna steak with light Pinot Noir
intermediate.fact: Dense, fatty tuna has the body to handle a light Pinot Noir — the fat neutralises tannin.

expert.q: Aged Comté cheese pairs exceptionally well with:
expert.fact: Comté and Vin Jaune share a Jura origin and matching nutty, oxidative character — a great regional match.

expert.q: "Congruent pairing" means:
opts: Matching similar flavour compounds in wine and food
Contrasting wine and food to create balance
Serving the wine that was cooked with the dish
expert.fact: Congruent = like with like: buttery Chardonnay with butter sauce, fruity Pinot with cherry reduction.

expert.q: Roquefort and Sauternes is a classic "contrast pairing". What makes it work?
opts: Sweet vs salty; rich vs acidic — opposites attract
Both are from the same region
The wine's tannins balance the cheese
expert.fact: The sweetness and acidity of Sauternes cuts through the salty fat of Roquefort — a contrast match.

expert.q: Why can Alsace Gewürztraminer work with mildly spiced Indian dishes?
opts: Residual sweetness tames spice; lychee/rose mirrors curry aromatics
expert.fact: Off-dry Gewürz has the sweetness to tame spice and the exotic aromatics to complement curry spices.

expert.q: Salt in food makes wine taste:
expert.fact: Salt suppresses bitterness and enhances fruit — it makes tannic wines taste smoother and rounder.

expert.q: Which umami-rich pairing demonstrates why vintage Port and Stilton is a classic?
opts: Port's sweetness and tannin balance the salty, savoury, fatty Stilton
The port's acidity cuts the cheese fat
expert.fact: Stilton's intense saltiness and fat are balanced by Port's sweetness, tannin and rich fruit — a great contrast match.
